soil-hist-040.title: World Congress of Soil Science, every four years
soil-hist-040.text: Every four years, soil scientists from around the world meet in one city. The World Congress of Soil Science is the conference of the {{ref:soil-hist-047}}, and it has kept that rhythm apart from a break for World War II. Only members may attend. The 1st congress met in Washington, DC, in 1927 and the 2nd in Leningrad in 1930. Since the 15th, in Acapulco, Mexico, about 2000 members have come each time. Editions of the World Reference Base were launched at congresses: the first at Montpellier in 1998, the fourth at Glasgow in 2022. The 23rd met in Nanjing, China, in 2026, and the 24th is planned for Toronto in 2030.

soil-hist-027.title: From a nutrient ledger to a science of soil
soil-hist-027.text: Soil was once treated like a bank account. Early agricultural chemists held a balance-sheet theory: soil was a more or less static store of plant nutrients that crops drew down and farmers could replace. Their concepts built on the chemistry of {{ref:soil-hist-004}}, refined by agricultural scientists in laboratories, greenhouses and small field plots. These workers rarely looked at soil below the depth of normal tillage. Early geologists accepted the balance sheet too. To them, soil was disintegrated rock, such as granite, sandstone or glacial till, modified by weathering and shaped into landforms. Many early soil surveyors were geologists, because only they had the field methods the work needed. So they saw soils mainly as weathering products of geologic formations. Surveys published before 1910 were strongly geological, and those of 1910 to 1920 added refinements without changing that foundation. The balance sheet ruled the laboratory and geology ruled the field. Many classrooms taught both until the late 1920s. Broader concepts came from {{ref:soil-hist-007}} and George Nelson Coffey in the United States and from Russian soil scientists. Yet the data behind them came from soil survey field work. The old balance sheet keeps some value today. Understanding soils, though, goes well beyond removing nutrients in crops and returning them as manure, lime and fertilizer.

soil-hist-035.title: Darwin's last book: the earthworm as a force of nature
soil-hist-035.text: Charles Darwin ended his scientific career with earthworms. His last scientific book, The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms, came out in October 1881, shortly before his death. It studied their habits and their part in forming and moving the soil. It carried his recurring theme: gradual changes over long periods can have large and sometimes surprising consequences. Darwin calculated that there were 53,767 earthworms per acre. He concluded that worms matter because they help decompose rock, slowly denude the land, preserve archaeological remains and improve soil for plant growth. He watched them drag leaves into their burrows by the most efficient end. Despite rudimentary sense organs, they showed complex, flexible behavior. The book was the first significant work on bioturbation, the mixing of soil by living things, though that word entered the soil literature only a hundred years later. It sold thousands of copies in its first few weeks.

soil-hist-038.title: 2015, the year the world was asked to notice soil
soil-hist-038.text: On 20 December 2013, the United Nations General Assembly declared 2015 the International Year of Soils. Its aim was to show how much soils matter for food security, agriculture, climate change mitigation, poverty alleviation and sustainable development. The FAO ran it within the Global Soil Partnership, which planned a website, a logo and activities, while organizations worldwide held local events. In the United States the USDA held a kick-off event, and the {{ref:soil-hist-050}} marked the year with monthly themes. It closed at FAO headquarters on 4 December 2015. The {{ref:soil-hist-047}} then proclaimed 2015–2024 the International Decade of Soils to continue the work.

soil-hist-077.title: Agricultural chemistry, the science behind the fertilizer bag
soil-hist-077.text: Most of the mass of dry soil is mineral matter. Agricultural chemistry is the chemistry of agriculture, especially its organic chemistry and biochemistry. When it analyzes soil, it looks at that mineral matter and at the organic matter too, including humic and fulvic acids. Its usual goal is to preserve or raise soil fertility, so that crops keep or improve their yield and quality. Time-honored organic fertilizers have largely given way to chemicals from mined phosphate rock and the Haber-Bosch process, which greatly raised crop production. Its pesticides raise yields as well, but they can contaminate ground and water and harm species they were never aimed at.

soil-hist-043.title: Soil Science Australia and its seven branches
soil-hist-043.text: Australia's soil scientists have had a professional home since 1955. The Australian Society of Soil Science Incorporated is a not-for-profit association for them and for others concerned with managing the country's soils. It was founded to advance soil science in professional, academic and technical fields, and in 2011 it adopted the public name Soil Science Australia. An elected Federal Council governs its seven branches. Members can gain accreditation as Certified Professional Soil Scientists. Its national conference meets every two years, jointly with the New Zealand Society of Soil Sciences every fourth year. In 2010 it co-hosted the 19th World Congress of Soil Science in Brisbane.

soil-hist-041.title: The World Soil Museum, a gallery of soil profiles
soil-hist-041.text: In Wageningen, in the Netherlands, the world's major soil types stand side by side. The World Soil Museum displays soil profile monoliths, preserved vertical slices of real soil profiles. It is managed by {{ref:soil-hist-049}}, an independent science-based foundation. It began as the International Soil Museum, at the request of UNESCO and the International Society of Soil Science, to support the FAO-UNESCO Soil Map of the World. Some 80 monoliths are on display. A much larger collection of some 1000, from over 70 countries, waits in its repository. Each comes with a horizon-by-horizon description and data. Visitors see examples of the 32 WRB Reference Soil Groups, a section on Dutch soils and soils much changed by long human use.

soil-hist-044.title: The Soil and Water Conservation Society
soil-hist-044.text: At a Chicago meeting on 11 November 1941, {{ref:soil-hist-019}} and three others proposed a new society. Its first minutes date from 16 February 1943, and it was formed that year as the Soil Conservation Society of America. In 1987 it took its present name. The Soil and Water Conservation Society is a professional and scientific membership society that fosters the science and art of managing natural resources sustainably. It publishes the bimonthly, peer-reviewed {{ref:soil-found-113}}. One source gives 1945 as the year it was formed.

soil-hist-031.title: From word pictures to measurements: building Soil Taxonomy
soil-hist-031.text: A soil class is only useful if two scientists would put the same soil in it. That was the weakness of the system of {{ref:soil-hist-009}} and of the 1938 USDA system. Their classes were described qualitatively, not in terms that different scientists could apply consistently. Neither linked its higher classes, defined by how soils form, to the soil series used in US soil mapping. A 1949 modification fixed some flaws. It also showed that the system's concepts and principles needed reappraisal. More than 15 years of work under {{ref:soil-hist-024}} produced a new, quantitative system. It was made official for the {{ref:soil-hist-051}} in 1965 and published in 1975 as Soil Taxonomy. The United States adopted it, and many other nations used it for their own classification.

soil-hist-028.title: When Russian scientists made soil a natural body
soil-hist-028.text: For a long time, soil counted as dead ground. It was seen as a product of physical and chemical changes in rock, a substrate from which plants take mineral nutrients. From 1870 a Russian school led by {{ref:soil-hist-001}} and N. M. Sibirtsev saw it differently. Soils, they held, are independent natural bodies with properties of their own. Each soil's unique properties come from a unique combination of climate, living matter, parent material, relief and time. Instead of inferring those properties from rocks or climate, they read the combined effect in the soil's own morphology, its visible form and layers. Considering all properties together, as one natural body, made a science of soil possible. The ideas are called revolutionary. Americans learned of them through a 1914 textbook in German by {{ref:soil-hist-008}}, and especially through its English translation of 1927 by {{ref:soil-hist-009}}. Some enthusiasts thought soil study could now ignore geology and agricultural chemistry. In fact the new concept made those sciences more useful. Morphology gave a firm basis for turning observations, experiments and experience into principles that predict how soils behave.

soil-hist-029.title: Putting the soil profile first, in America
soil-hist-029.text: In the United States, the Russian idea was rebuilt around the soil profile. Led by {{ref:soil-hist-009}}, the American version put the individual profile ahead of external soil features and surface geology. Classification, he insisted, must rest on morphology, not on theories of soil genesis, which he saw as ephemeral and dynamic. His 1935 classification relied on a "normal soil", formed in equilibrium on a landscape where downward erosion keeps pace with soil formation. The focus had costs. Early soil scientists overlooked how much soils vary even within a small area, which seriously reduced the value of their maps. Material without a genetic profile, such as recent alluvium, seemed not to be soil at all. After 1930, studies moved from single pits to trenches or series of pits. Soils were described by ranges of properties around a central concept, not by one typical profile. Yet through the 1930s, soil formation was still explained by loosely conceived regional processes such as podzolization, laterization and calcification.

soil-hist-045.title: Germany's soil society, founded in Berlin in 1926
soil-hist-045.text: In Berlin in 1926, German soil scientists formed a section of the International Soil Science Society. After the Second World War the group was re-formed in Wiesbaden. Today the Deutsche Bodenkundliche Gesellschaft, or DBG, is a non-profit society of soil science experts and others interested in the field. It has around 2000 members, with headquarters in Göttingen since 2012. Its meeting every two years is the main forum in German-speaking countries for new findings in soil science. With the German Society of Plant Nutrition, it publishes the Journal of Plant Nutrition and Soil Science.

soil-hist-039.title: World Soil Day, every 5 December
soil-hist-039.text: Each year, 5 December is set aside for the ground underfoot. World Soil Day celebrates the importance of soil in people's lives. The {{ref:soil-hist-047}} proposed the date in 2002. The UN General Assembly designated it in December 2013, when it also declared 2015 the International Year of Soils. The {{ref:soil-hist-048}} and the American Society of Agronomy invite the public to keep celebrating it every year. The FAO runs the #WorldSoilDay hashtag and campaigns such as "Stop soil erosion, Save our future", with activities for students, farmers, teachers and others.

soil-hist-042.title: The world's first soil museum, in Saint Petersburg
soil-hist-042.text: The world's first museum of soil science opened in Saint Petersburg in 1904, a year after its founder died. Its founder was {{ref:soil-hist-001}}, commonly called the father of soil science and leader of the Russian school. He set it up in 1902. He had begun his large collection of soil samples in 1880. The V.V. Dokuchaev Central Museum of Soil now holds about 330 soil monoliths, from the Arctic to New Zealand. Expeditions bring new ones every year.

soil-hist-046.title: Park Grass, a hay field watched since 1856
soil-hist-046.text: One hay field in Hertfordshire has been monitored since 1856. The Park Grass Experiment, at {{ref:soil-hist-053}}, was set up to test how fertilizers and manures affect hay yields. It is one of the longest-running experiments in modern science. Its treatments changed the plant make-up and ecology of the 28,000 m² field. That made it a resource for studying natural selection and biodiversity. It showed how plant species richness, biomass and pH are related. It also showed that ordinary field trials probably underestimate long-term threats such as soil acidification. Its archive of soil and hay samples has even been used to track atmospheric pollution, including nuclear fallout.

soil-hist-037.title: How earthworms slowly bury stones and ruins
soil-hist-037.text: In December 1842, Charles Darwin spread broken chalk over a pasture near Down House. It ended up buried 18 centimeters deep, a rate of 6 millimeters per year. Earthworms bring up earth from below and leave it on the surface as castings, so objects on top slowly sink. Darwin estimated how much earth they raise from such burial rates and by weighing the castings produced over set times. He found the outer stones of Stonehenge partly buried. Worms, dust and soil wash, he concluded, had buried Roman ruins such as Abinger and Silchester. Rain and wind move castings downslope. Meanwhile the worms' humic acids and the stones they swallow help break down rock.

soil-hist-036.title: Darwin's first worm paper, read in 1837
soil-hist-036.text: At Maer Hall, Josiah Wedgwood showed his nephew Charles Darwin some curious ground. Lime and cinders spread there years before now lay beneath a layer of loam, and Wedgwood suggested earthworms were the cause. On 1 November 1837, Darwin read a paper to the Geological Society of London on the role of earthworms in forming soil. William Buckland backed its publication as "a new Geological Power". He rejected, though, Darwin's idea that chalkland formed the same way. The paper appeared in the society's Proceedings in 1838 and, with a woodcut, in its Transactions in 1840.

soil-hist-033.title: Bioturbation: a word from 1952 for an idea from Darwin
soil-hist-033.text: Darwin was first to see how much burrowing creatures matter for soil processes and landforms, and he devoted his last scientific book to it. In 1891 the geologist Nathaniel Shaler extended the idea to soil disturbed by ants and trees. The name came later. Rudolf Richter coined bioturbation in 1952 for sediment structures made by living organisms. Since the 1980s soil geomorphologists, who study soils and landforms together, have used it widely. There is now ample evidence for Darwin's conclusions. In many areas, burrowing animals and plants are major agents of soil formation.

soil-hist-030.title: Soil formation becomes a measurable science
soil-hist-030.text: From about 1940, soil formation stopped being one vague process. It became many interrelated physical, chemical and biological processes, open to quantitative study. A 1941 book by {{ref:soil-hist-010}}, Factors of Soil Formation: A System of Quantitative Pedology, summarized many basic principles of modern soil science up to that date. Since then time has gained much more weight among the soil-forming factors. Geomorphology is used to find how long material has undergone soil formation. Advances in soil chemistry, physics, mineralogy and biology added new tools. Attention moved from gross traits of the whole soil to the co-varying detail of its parts, down to grain-to-grain relationships.

soil-hist-034.title: Soil organic matter and a textbook theory under fire
soil-hist-034.text: Some of what soil science long taught about organic matter now looks shaky. Flaws first showed in 1999, when soil models could not account for the large charcoal component of Chernozems. In 2016 soil science textbooks began to address the need to abandon long-accepted but outdated concepts. As of 2021, few yet understood that the classic textbook theory of how soil organic matter accumulates "has been proven mostly false". The question is not settled. The humification theory, which pictures organic matter turning into stable humus, still appears in textbooks, while some researchers argue it is wrong.

soil-hist-032.title: Soil surveys move beyond the farm
soil-hist-032.text: Soil surveys were once made almost entirely for farmers, ranchers and foresters. That held until about 1950. Yet some states saw their value for highway planning by the late 1920s, and in the 1930s and 1940s they put soil interpretations into highway engineers' manuals. Then nonfarm uses of soil grew rapidly in the 1950s and 1960s. That created a great need for information on how soils affect those uses. The impact on soil survey was immense, especially during the 1960s.

openers.hist: Soil science is a young science with a long backstory. Its ideas first grew from the chemistry of {{ref:soil-hist-004}}, tested in laboratories, greenhouses and small field plots. From 1870 a Russian school led by {{ref:soil-hist-001}} recast soils as independent natural bodies, and {{ref:soil-hist-009}} adapted that idea for America. Meanwhile Charles Darwin, in his 1881 book, showed earthworms forming and moving the soil. This part follows those people and their classifications, and the societies, museums and congresses that carry the work today, from a soil museum in Wageningen to a United Nations year for soils in 2015.
openers.history-of-soil-science: How did soil become a subject of its own? Its first concepts were built on the chemistry of {{ref:soil-hist-004}} and refined by agricultural scientists in laboratories, greenhouses and small field plots. From 1870 the Russian school treated soils as independent natural bodies, and an American adaptation put the individual soil profile first. Later the qualitative classifications of {{ref:soil-hist-009}} and of 1938 gave way to a quantitative system built under {{ref:soil-hist-024}}. Along the way, Darwin's earthworms, museums, congresses, societies and a whole year for soils each left their mark.

reviews.history-of-soil-science: Soil science began with two narrow views: a chemist's balance sheet of nutrients and a geologist's picture of weathered rock. The Russian school recast soils as natural bodies, an American adaptation put the profile first, and the quantitative Soil Taxonomy replaced word-picture classes in 1965. Darwin, from his 1837 paper to his 1881 book, showed that earthworms bury objects and remake the ground, an idea later named bioturbation. Park Grass, two soil museums, congresses and societies keep long records and bring scientists together. Even now the science revises itself, as the old textbook theory of soil organic matter comes under challenge.
